content:
Earlier this year, I traded a battery-powered push mower for an iPhone-controlled robotic mower. That machine builds a virtual map by letting you manually drive it around your yard's perimeter. Once set up, it takes care of mowing on a schedule automatically.

I've been testing another system lately called the TerraMow V1000. It takes a completely different approach to navigation, and after weeks of testing, I think it may be the easier choice for a lot of people.

Camera-driven automatic mapping

The biggest difference between the TerraMow V1000 and the Anthbot M9 I reviewed earlier this year is how each machine understands your yard.

The Anthbot M9 uses an RTK reference station for positioning. Setup required me to manually drive the mower around the perimeter with my iPhone to build an initial map.

The TerraMow V1000 uses a system the company calls TerraVision 2.0. Through three cameras, the mower automatically maps your lawn and navigates without the need for buried boundary wires or a separate RTK antenna.

The automatic approach takes longer to build the initial map. But I think it may be simpler for anyone who isn't fond of hands-on tech setup.

To put that idea to the test, I had my mom, who's in another state, set up and use the TerraMow V1000 on her own without my help. She reported that everything worked fine. I'm less sure she would have had the patience to manually drive the robot through the full perimeter and mark zones to avoid.

Automatic mapping did trigger one minor issue in my front yard. My lawn has no fence or physical separation from my neighbor's lawn, so TerraMow initially included a portion of my neighbor's yard in my map.

I fixed it by marking the area as a no-go zone in the app. Still, if there's no clear visual boundary between lawns, the initial mapping process warrants extra attention.

Watching through the mower's cameras

TerraMow's cameras also enable one of my favorite features. The iPhone app can show you in real time what the mower sees as it works.

During testing, I kept the view open in a large window via iPhone Mirroring on my Mac. That let me work inside while watching the mower's view of its movement around the backyard.

It's not essential for automated mowing, but it makes the robot more fun to be around and occasionally helps explain why it slows down or avoids certain obstacles. The Anthbot M9 doesn't offer a similar camera view.

The two iPhone apps have a lot in common otherwise. Both support scheduled jobs, mowing pattern adjustments, creating zones, marking no-go areas, and remote-controlling the mower.

TerraMow has one particularly clever design for that last feature. In addition to the traditional left and right virtual sticks, its app offers a single-hand joystick mode. You hold your iPhone normally and use your thumb to steer the mower.

Manually driving the mower with your iPhone isn't the main purpose of either system. Ideally, the robot runs on its schedule without any input. Still, TerraMow's joystick is genuinely useful for cleaning up missed patches.

At times, it almost feels like I'm controlling the robot with my mind (in a good way). I can hold the phone at my side, walk alongside the mower with just subtle thumb movements, and it follows my direction.

Every robotic mower app should copy this control scheme.

More aggressive mowing

The TerraMow V1000 also feels more aggressive than the Anthbot M9. During testing, it cut lower and was louder while working.

I wouldn't call TerraMow noisy, but the difference is noticeable. The Anthbot can run quietly enough that you forget it's there, even when it keeps mowing after dark with its headlights on.

Because TerraMow relies on camera navigation, it needs daylight to operate reliably. That makes daytime scheduling more important.

The V1000 itself feels solid and substantial, and it's larger than the Anthbot M9. TerraMow includes a protective garage that covers the charging dock, while Anthbot's garage is sold separately.

Most importantly, TerraMow performed reliably. I relied on it for weeks without ever needing to step in for normal mowing duties.

When adaptive mapping gets too clever

The same visual intelligence that makes TerraMow easy to set up occasionally works against it.

The mower continuously adjusts its map based on what it sees. Saving those changes after each session takes a while, during which the app temporarily can't do anything else.

I also ran into an interesting edge case after several days of heavy rain. A portion of the yard collected standing water, and TerraMow reasonably avoided that spot the next time it ran.

The skipped circular patch grew taller grass as a result. Over time, the mower seemed to treat the growth there as something to keep avoiding, even after the ground dried out, and that area didn't get mowed.

I fixed it by manually driving the mower over the taller grass using the app's remote control. Once that patch returned to looking like lawn, automated mowing resumed there normally.

Regular edging also helps TerraMow reach its boundaries cleanly. Otherwise, tall grass along a fuzzy border may be misinterpreted as an obstacle rather than part of the mowing area.

The Anthbot's approach, by contrast, is less adaptive. It relies more heavily on the boundaries and obstacles I define myself. That takes more effort up front, but it also avoids the map "changing its mind" and skipping a patch of grass.

9to5Mac Take

After using both systems, I lean toward TerraMow's camera-based approach for most people.

Burying boundary wire is a complete non-starter for me, and installing an RTK reference station adds another piece of hardware to position, power, and maintain. TerraMow avoids both.

Its visual navigation isn't flawless. The initial mapping takes longer, an invisible property line needed a manual fix, and its adaptive behavior once mistook overgrown weeds for a permanent obstacle.

These issues are manageable. In return, the TerraMow V1000 delivers easier setup, reliable automated mowing, an engaging live camera view, and the best manual driving experience I've had with a robotic mower.

I genuinely enjoy yard work, but mowing is the most repetitive part of it. Handing it off to a robot frees me up to focus more on landscaping, edging, and the finer details while keeping the lawn tidy.

The TerraMow V1000 does that job well and earns a recommendation, especially for anyone who wants automated mowing without burying wire, installing an RTK antenna, or walking the full yard manually from an iPhone.

Amazon is currently selling the TerraMow V1000 for $999, with a $200 coupon available on the site. You can also buy it from TerraMow's official website.
